And the financial crisis was the real estate market, and the real estate issues were in Florida. And pretty much everybody I knew was impacted by this. This crisis. So I, as a student of economics, really challenged myself to just understand what the heck was going on between Washington and Wall street and why that was impacting my family and my community and everybody I knew. And what came out of that was I was quite disturbed at the state of our economic affairs and how we got there and felt we should have better accountability. And I dedicated my career to working in public policy and moved to D.C. to fight for a better economic future for my generation and those that will come after me. So in working on Capitol Hill, I learned about Bitcoin. And as an economist looking at this virtual currency that was not controlled or created by a government or. Or a corporation or a group of people, that was just a fascinating concept. And the more I learned about Bitcoin and the more I learned about blockchain technology, the more I felt that all of the things that I was fighting for, from a policy perspective, from a more transparent financial system to a more safe and secure and efficient way to remit payment globally, I felt that Bitcoin represented all of those things. And I just became a huge advocate. And I feel this is the most important technology I will ever see in my entire life. And I've dedicated my entire focus on helping support the growth of this technology. So that's when we founded the Chamber of Digital Commerce. And our space and what we're trying to contribute to this industry is to be a reputable resource based in our nation's capital that can work with policymakers and help just answer all the questions that they have. There's a lot of fear, there's a lot of anxiety, there's a lot of skepticism and weird things about bitcoin and crypto and blockchain. We want to educate them, we want to make sure they have the right information, and we want to make sure our voice is heard in conversations that are going to impact the growth of our ecosystem. So that's what we set out to do and we've been pretty busy ever since.

speaker: A

text: So one of the things that's been really interesting is seeing the Federal Reserve's response to cryptocurrencies the very first, I mean, at the beginning of bitcoin and the crypto ecosystem, a lot of people were really interested in what is the Fed's response going to be to this new currency. And the Fed didn't say a word until 2013, when Janet Yellen was testifying in her semiannual address to Congress. And Senator Joe Manchin had asked Janet Yellen, the chair of the Fed, if she could ban Bitcoin because he was adamantly against it because of all the illicit that was right during Silk Road. So people using Bitcoin for illicit purposes, he thought it should be shut down. Can the Fed do that? And her response was, the Fed has no jurisdiction over Bitcoin. And like, that was it. And she just moved on to the next question. And like, that was all we heard from arguably one of the most powerful institutions. And it really didn't give us much insight at all in their thinking. And fast forward to today. So just a few years later, it hasn't really been, I mean, it seems in bitcoin time, it seemed. Seems like a long time, but in just a few short years. The new chair of the Fed, Jay Powell, just last year was asked about Bitcoin in his semiannual address to Congress. And he said, it's like digital gold. So a store of value is one of the key use cases of Bitcoin. And to have the chair of the Fed validate that this technology is used for that purpose, I thought was probably one of the most important endorsements it could ever get. So just to see that huge change in their thinking in a short amount of time has been really amazing to see and really shows the true importance of what this technology is and what it has the potential to become.

text: Yeah, so two points there. As someone who worked on Capitol Hill on financial services issues, my job was to meet with all the trade groups and the lobbyists and the special interest groups and all the issues Congress is deliberating on. And the incumbents, you know, the banks, your established financial services companies, they have just unbelievable amounts of resources in these policy conversations. And I always felt that it is important that we engage them in the process because their voice is so big and so powerful. To just ignore that would be naive and a huge misstep. So by creating an inclusive platform. And so for me, I've always wanted the Chamber and everything that I do in this space to be as inclusive as possible. We welcome all those in our platform that share our values. Depending. Many different companies are using and innovating in many different ways. And all of those who are dedicated to growing this ecosystem and developing this technology, please be a part of these important policy conversations that we're having. But we are really unique in that. I think we probably are one of the only groups in this space that has brought together the technology companies and the incumbents into one platform. And to be able to get consensus amongst that group on the policy positions impacting crypto, that is a huge feat. But it also gives us an unbelievably powerful voice as we're advocating for the growth of this ecosystem. And you do raise a good point. So if you have really big companies, like public companies, and you have really small companies, small startups, they don't have the same amount of resources to contribute to public policy things. And I certainly understand that every single. We represent over 200 companies. Every single company has the same voice. Larger companies do pay larger membership dues, because they should. But every company has an equal voice. And our default position when we create a policy position, we go to the Hill or we go to Congress or the agencies, and we're advocating for that is always going to be what's best for the ecosystem as a whole, not what's best for this member or that member or this group or that group. We're advocating for the growth of the entire ecosystem. So that's where our position is always going to default to. And sometimes not everybody agrees on that because it can disenfranchise one company over another. But we want to do the right thing. We want to have an inclusive platform. And we're always going to promote the growth of this ecosystem over the growth of one particular company who may or may not have more resources than another. So all are encouraged and welcome to participate. And we ensure that what we do is in line with that mission.
speaker: B

text: So what is the upside for industry? I've talked a lot about engaging as well and how to do that and how to be effective in doing that, no matter what the size of your business is. So what is in it for the industry? What is the upside for participating in these policy discussions?
speaker: A

text: These conversations are happening whether you want to be a part of them or not, in the most powerful offices in the world today are debating and writing regulations that are going to dictate the future of this ecosystem. So you have a choice. You can either be a part of the conversation and try to shape it in a direction that's going to be beneficial, or you can have it shaped around you. And I can guarantee you that the former is going to end up in a better position than the latter. And also for younger companies, for startups, for smaller organizations, being a part of a trade group like the Chamber, where you can share resources with other companies is a great way to have your voice heard without having to bring in your own team of public policy experts. So there's a lot of resources you can share off the chambers platform to ensure you have a meaningful voice, but doing it in a way that makes sense for a small company.

text: Yeah, and one of the other things that I wanted to just mention, we also operate on a form of radical transparency. So all of our members are posted on our website. So anyone and everybody wants to know exactly who is part of the chambers platform. And also all of our policy positions are all posted on our website. So every single letter we've ever submitted to a government organization, we put it online. So if you want to learn more about exactly what our positions are and exactly what we're saying to government, we want everyone to be able to share in that knowledge and have access to that in the spirit of transparency. In terms of what some of the issues are, it's kind of interesting. So I'll just focus on the US and in the US we have this two party system with Republicans and Democrats and both sides kind of care about two very different things. Republicans really seem to be very sympathetic to the business arguments that this is an incredibly important technology. We want the United States to be at the lead of developing innovation of this technology. We want US Companies to be leaders in the blockchain ecosystem. And we want to give them the regulatory clarity and certainty they need to be able to establish businesses and grow and create jobs and create economic prosperity here in the United States. Republicans seem to be more sympathetic to that conversation and have been quite active in helping us get there on a number of specific policy issues, whether it's AML issues or tax issues. You're dealing with the securities and Exchange Commission or so on and so forth. On the Democrat side, it's very different types of conversations. So they have concerns about investor protections and consumer protections. Bitcoin has been highly volatile asset over the past, well since its inception. And we've seen huge price spikes during a bull market and then a lot of wealth being evaporated through the cycles. And there's natural concerns there, but that's also the ebb and flow of crypto. So they're very much in tune with ensuring that, yes, of course, the United States is a leader in this technology, but that we're also creating appropriate protections to ensure we have a healthy, functioning marketplace. So there is a balance and there are legitimate concerns that need to be addressed. And getting there has always been an ongoing conversation.

text: So education is the biggest challenge in having these policy conversations and learning about bitcoin and cryptocurrencies and blockchain technology is something that takes more than like a 15 minute briefing. They're used to, like coming in, you have a quick ask, you deliver like a one page with a summary. But it's been hard to do that if nobody really knows what it is you're talking about. So first we have to hire these people to want to understand this technology. And then once they have a basic degree of education, then we can start talking about the policy issues. So continuing to refine the messaging and making the learning process easier. I mean, when I first learned about Bitcoin, I probably spent an entire year just reading all sorts of whatever I could find on the Internet. And it took me quite a bit of time just to understand how it works, let alone how the policy implications are going to impact this technology.

speaker: A

text: So my most memorable moment would have been the day we announced the formation of the chamber, which we launched on July 19th of 2014. So just about six years ago. And we did it at the North American Bitcoin Conference. It was an industry event in Chicago. And Mo Levin, who organized the event, he allowed me to make a special announcement at the very start of the event. So I'm in there and nobody really knows what I'm about to say, and probably nobody really knows me either. And I get up and I just said, look, we're launching the Chamber of Digital Commerce. It's launched today. All are welcome to be a part of this. We are here to serve as a resource to policymakers and to address all these regulatory challenges that we have as a community. And this is 2014. So the community looked very different then than it does it did today. There was no one in DC working on crypto stuff at all. We were the first there. I mean, most of the people were like cyberpunks, anarcho capitalist. The whole narrative of Bitcoin was like, we're going to overthrow the government, we're going to overthrow the banks, and bitcoin's going to. It was a really different space. I'm like, either of these people are going to bulldoze me and maybe assassinate me. I don't know. I was so nervous. I really did not know how people would respond. And to my surprise, everyone cheered, stood and clapped. Like, people were like, this is a great idea. So it was probably the most relieving moment of my life. I wasn't sure how folks were going to take it, but it has been amazing that there are a lot of people that do understand we have to engage on the policy. As much as we're investing on building out the tech and building out our teams and our communities and our platforms, you also have to invest in those policy issues, because if you don't get those right, it's going to put huge roadblocks. So it's. Yeah, I mean, it's been a total whirlwind.

I'm happy to be your supporter and advocate in that journey, as I've had to do with building the Chamber as a nonprofit. And the second is be kind to each other. There's a lot of competition in this space, but at the end of the day, we are all on the same team. We are all still part of the same community.
